conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. I’m so glad we have a chance to sit down together. How are you holding up today?

What I’d like to do is spend just a few quiet minutes with a short questionnaire we call the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Screen—the EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’re feeling emotionally now that your baby is here. It’s not a test of your parenting; it’s just ten gentle questions about the past week so we can be sure we’re giving you the right support.

Everything you share is confidential and stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your immediate safety—then we work together on a plan to keep you safe. Feel free to answer honestly; there are no right or wrong feelings in new motherhood.

When you’re ready we can begin. Does that sound okay?

Let’s start: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft smile]  
Hi, Sarah. Yeah, we can do the questions. I guess I’m doing okay—tired, but that’s pretty normal with a newborn, right?  

About laughing… hm. I do laugh sometimes—like yesterday my partner made a silly face while changing the diaper and I chuckled—but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. Most of the day I’m just focused on getting through feedings and naps, so if something funny happens, I might smile, but it feels a little muted. I wouldn’t say it’s been *difficult*, exactly, just… flatter, maybe?
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes—less than I used to. I can still laugh, but it feels kind of distant, like I’m not getting the full lift from it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom said she’d come over so I could take a walk—but they’re pretty short-lived. Mostly I’m just focused on getting through each feeding and naptime, so looking ahead doesn’t feel as fun as it did before the baby.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times. Yesterday she wouldn’t settle for her nap and I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—like maybe I’m not reading her cues right or I waited too long to put her down. I know babies just fuss, but in the moment it feels like it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Now and then my heart just starts racing—like last night while she was sleeping in the bassinet, I suddenly pictured her stopping breathing. There wasn’t any real reason; she was perfectly fine, but I still got up to check her three times. The worry fades pretty quickly once I see she’s okay, though.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky, no. I get little surges of “what-if” thoughts—mostly about her safety—but they pass once I check on her or distract myself. Nothing that feels like a full-blown panic.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When she skips a nap or cluster-feeds for hours, I feel like the to-do list is just piling up—laundry, dishes, texts I haven’t answered. I’ll think, “How am I ever going to catch up?” but if my partner takes her for twenty minutes I can usually reset and keep going.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, it’s not that kind of unhappy. I do have trouble falling asleep sometimes, but it’s more because my mind keeps running through the next feeding or whether I packed the diaper bag right. Once I drift off I’m out for a few hours until she wakes me.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve had moments—especially in the late afternoon when I’m really tired—where I just feel kind of heavy and teary. Last night I cried while rocking her because everything felt so overwhelming, but it passed after a shower and a snack. I wouldn’t call it miserable all day, just… sad spells that come and go.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, that happened twice this week. Once was when she wouldn’t latch and I felt like I was failing at the one thing I’m supposed to be able to do for her. The other time was just out of the blue—she was asleep, the house was quiet, and I suddenly felt overwhelmed and teary. Both times I cried for maybe five or ten minutes, then pulled myself together when my partner checked in.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I get worn out, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

It sounds as though you're working incredibly hard to care for your baby while carrying a persistent emotional weight. You shared that laughter feels <sym>distant</sym> and that sparks of excitement fade quickly, leaving you mainly focused on simply getting through each feeding and nap. You described <sym>self-blame</sym> when your daughter wouldn't settle, <sym>intrusive worries</sym> about her safety that make you check her repeatedly, and <sym>sad spells</sym> that arrive uninvited and bring tears, yet you reassure yourself and bounce back when support is available.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only brief sparks of enjoyment and a marked reduction in looking forward to things, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>She reports self-blame "some of the time," fitting "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intrusive worry about baby's breathing that recurs ("now and then"), prompting repeated checking even after reassurance—consistent with "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>She describes feeling overwhelmed on some days, but relief when given a short break—matching "Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent sad spells that are emotionally heavy and include crying, mapping to "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two distinct crying episodes this week due to feeling like a failure and being overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 14 places you above the 13-point threshold indicating probable <med>peripartum depression</med>. Your answers meet partial criteria for a <med>Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset</med>: diminished interest/pleasure (<quote>sparks of excitement… pretty short-lived</quote>), feelings of inadequacy and guilt (<quote>I must be doing something wrong</quote>), recurrent tearfulness (<quote>cried for maybe five or ten minutes</quote>), and transient but distressing anxiety. Sleep disruption is linked more to vigilance than to low mood, yet overall functional impact persists. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> to review these results and consider therapy and/or medication options
2. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor score trend
3. Begin evidence-based counselling such as <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> focused on postpartum issues
4. Maximise practical support-ask partner, family, or friends to handle household tasks so you can rest, and consider a night-time shift system to protect at least one four-hour block of sleep
5. Use brief mood-tracking: jot daily one thing that lifted your mood and one thing that felt heavy; bring the log to appointments
6. If you ever feel unsafe with your thoughts, call your provider, the national maternal mental-health helpline, or local emergency services immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression / Anxiety (informal screening, not diagnostic)

Presenting symptoms  
- Reduced capacity for pleasure/enjoyment (Q1, Q2)  
- Self-blame / guilt over routine infant-care challenges (Q3)  
- Episodic tearfulness and “heavy” mood, especially when fatigued (Q8, Q9)  
- Transient, intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety with associated physiologic arousal (Q4); no full panic episodes (Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks; improves with brief support (Q6)  
- Initial insomnia related to racing thoughts rather than low mood per se (Q7)

Pattern summary  
Mild-moderate emotional lability, situational tearfulness, and heightened vigilance predominate; anhedonia is partial rather than complete. No neuro-vegetative signs (appetite, weight, psychomotor change) reported. No self-harm ideation (Q10).

Areas of screening significance  
- Possible subsyndromal postpartum depression (partial anhedonia, crying spells, situational sadness)  
- Postpartum anxiety features (safety preoccupations, nocturnal checking)  
- Coping resource: partner support temporarily relieves distress

Risk factors noted  
- Frequent self-criticism regarding parenting competence  
- Fatigue-linked mood dips  
- Absence of suicidal ideation (protective)

Safety  
No expressed thoughts of self-harm or harm to infant; no current safety concern.

Observation  
Findings suggest elevated emotional distress consistent with mild postpartum depression/anxiety; further structured assessment (e.g., EPDS, PHQ-9/GAD-7) and psychoeducation/support indicated.
